The Death of the Last Burji Heir

The premature death of the last legitimate heir to the Burji dynasty has left the Mamluk Sultanate as a sultanate without a sultan. An eternal regency has been established, an administrative monstrosity heavily criticized by the Mamluk 'Abbasid' Caliph in Cairo. However, outside our borders, most of the Muslim world rejects Cairo's claims, recognizing only the Caliph of Volzhariya in the north as the true leader of the faithful. With power fractured and legitimacy shattered, the empire begins to unravel.
An eternal regency begins. God save the state.
Eritrean Secession

Taking advantage of the total political paralysis in Cairo caused by the regency crisis, local leaders in Mamluk Tigray have coordinated an armed rebellion. Demanding immediate independence, they have seized the port of Massawa and severed all ties with the Sultanate.

Mesopotamia is engulfed in fire. For decades, the local Shia majority in Baghdad and Basra has suffered under the heavy-handed rule of Cairo, paying exorbitant taxes to a distant court that views them with constant suspicion. With the news of the permanent Mamluk regency and the hollow claims of the Cairo Caliphate, local Shia clerics and regional leaders have finally snapped. They have declared the Mamluk state illegitimate and formed a new sovereign government under the local Faisal Al-Mesopotami, aiming to break the shackles of centuries of Sunni Mamluk exploitation and secure a free state for their people.
The Wahhabi Uprising

Deep within the harsh Arabian desert, the fiercely independent tribes of Nejd have run out of patience with the corruption and leaderless decay in Cairo. Led by the fundamentalist House of Saud under the command of Saud Al-Wahhabi, the desert clans have organized a massive religious and political rebellion. Declaring that a sultanate without a true sultan has no right to demand tribute or loyalty, they have driven Mamluk tax collectors out of the interior, aiming to establish a state governed by the strict principles of the Wahhabi movement, free from foreign interference.
Zaydi Independence

The rugged and defensive highlands of Yemen have erupted into a coordinated anti-Mamluk war. The regional Zaydi imams, who have long held deep-seated spiritual and political grievances against the Cairo regime, have seized upon the permanent regency crisis to declare a sovereign state under Imam Yahya. The local population has mobilized en masse, fortifying the mountain passes and taking control of the vital ports along the coast. This open defiance directly threatens Mamluk dominance over the lucrative trade routes flowing through the Bab-el-Mandeb strait.
The Abbasid Restoration

The ultimate insult to Cairo's authority has come from the holy lands of the Hejaz. Capitalizing on the total administrative paralysis of the regency council, the highly influential House of Hashim has stepped forward to claim its historical birthright. Declaring that the leaderless and illegitimate Mamluk regime is no longer fit to hold or protect the sanctuaries of Islam, Abdullah Al-Abbasi has led a swift take-over of Mecca and Medina. Backed by local clans, they have established an independent state, shattering what little prestige Egypt still held in the Muslim world.
The Syrian Rebellion

From Damascus to the northern walls of Aleppo, the wealthy and strategic region of Syria has risen in total defiance. For years, the Syrian merchant elites and regional nobility have resented their complete political subordination to Egypt, viewing themselves as second-class citizens in an empire they heavily fund. Coordinated by a branch of the prominent Hashim dynasty under Faisal Al-Hashimi, local regiments and urban populations have united to expel the Mamluk military garrisons, demanding the immediate establishment of a sovereign Syrian kingdom and a permanent end to Cairo's administrative stranglehold.
The Tunisian Revolt

The westernmost borderlands of the empire have finally fractured. For years, Tunisia was left isolated and neglected by a distant government in Cairo, forced to defend its borders with local resources while being drained of its economic output. Seeing the empire slide into a permanent regency crisis, the regional administrative council under Youssef Al-Tunisi has decided that loyalty to a dead dynasty is a suicide pact. Severing all communication and legal ties with Egypt, they have raised the flag of a sovereign Tunisian state, forcing out the remaining loyalist officials.
The Palestine Question

Palestine has long been managed as a semi-autonomous Taifa, a political compromise that allowed local councils in Jerusalem and Jaffa to handle day-to-day administrative matters. However, this autonomy was an illusion, as the region possessed zero financial independence—every coin collected in taxes was forcefully centralized in Cairo, leaving local infrastructure to decay while Palestinian resources funded the lavish lifestyles of the Mamluk elite. With central authority fractured by the regency crisis, local councils led by Ali Al-Hashimi have declared an independent government, refusing to let another coin leave the Levant.
